title: Hydrogen embrittlement in automotive steels: a review
abstract: Abstract Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) is a widely recognised phenomenon that can expressively impact high-strength materials. In particular, high-strength steels are susceptible to delayed fracture, a form of hydrogen embrittlement that may occur during vehicle service. HE can trigger fracture, accelerate subcritical crack growth, and result in catastrophic failure, ultimately reducing mechanical properties like strength, toughness, and ductility. Hydrogen can penetrate materials either through electrochemical reactions or exposure to high-pressure hydrogen environments. To evaluate its impact on mechanical properties and measure the absorbed hydrogen content, several techniques are employed, such as Slow Strain Rate Testing (SSRT), Linearly Increasing Stress Testing (LIST), and Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS). In automotive steels, a typical amount of hydrogen can be found in the range of 1 to 5 ppm (parts per million) by weight, but this can vary depending on the type of steel and its processing. The extent of mechanical degradation is not a standard metric but can evident as a significant loss of ductility, such as a loss in ductility by 30% or more which can depend on many factors like stress, hydrogen concentration, and environmental conditions. Several mechanisms responsible for HE is also explored. This paper summarizes phenomenon of HE, HE mechanisms and prevention methods which retard the process of hydrogen diffusion, subcritical crack growth, techniques to quantify absorbed hydrogen.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In the past many years, the demand for high-strength steels has risen significantly across various industries, particularly in the automotive sector, due to their superior mechanical properties. Automobiles play an essential role in daily life, and key features such as excellent ductility, high tensile strength, fracture toughness and energy absorption during impact are crucial for ensuring safety in car body design and construction. One of the major concerns of the automotive industry is reducing vehicle weight while enhancing crashworthiness, aiming to lower CO2 emissions by improving fuel efficiency, all while maintaining the same level of strength and toughness at the lowest possible cost [ 1 ,  2 ]. While aluminium is often considered for its lightweight properties, its lower stiffness and higher cost present major drawbacks compared to steel. To address these limitations and meet performance requirements, high-strength steels have been developed, offering an optimal combination of good strength and less weight.

The susceptibility to HE tends to increase as the strength of steel rises, particularly when it exceeds approximately 1200 MPa [ 3 ,  4 ]. However, as the yield stress increases, other mechanical properties often decline. Generally, the susceptibility of materials to brittle fracture increases, especially when exposed to different environments, leading to phenomena such as hydrogen embrittlement, stress corrosion cracking (SCC), and corrosion-fatigue. High-strength steels, in particular, have a greater number of potential crack initiation sites and experience higher stress levels at these sites, making them more prone to hydrogen embrittlement [ 5 ].

Some of the most important types of advanced high-strength steels contain High Strength Low Alloy (HSLA), Transformation Induced Plasticity (TRIP), Dual Phase (DP), Complex Phase (CP), Bainitic steel and Martensitic steels. DP steel is a mixture of martensitic phase dispersed in a ferrite matrix, resulting in the combined effect of both low yield and high tensile strength. TRIP steel offers a balance of good formability and high strength due to the conversion of metastable retained austenite (RA) into martensite during loading, thereby enhancing its mechanical properties. CP steel features a microstructure of very fine ferrite in combination with a high number of hard phases which can be strengthened by the fine precipitation of elements like niobium, titanium, and vanadium. Bainitic steel contains a microstructure of fine ferrite and retained austenite, which improves its strength and toughness. HSLA steel is characterised by a ferrite-cementite microstructure and is further strengthened through precipitation hardening from elements like titanium and niobium. Martensitic steel undergoes a near-complete transformation from high-temperature austenite into martensite during quenching, giving it exceptional strength.

Hydrogen embrittlement occurs when a material comes into contact with hydrogen, leading to hydrogen adsorption on the surface and subsequent absorption into the material from the environment. Even trace amounts of hydrogen, as minute as a few parts per million (ppm), can cause cracking and a marginal loss of ductility, especially in high-strength steels. This undesirable phenomenon can ultimately have a harmful impression on the mechanical properties of the steel [ 6 ,  7 ].

Hydrogen that has been absorbed usually diffuses between grains or, more frequently, along grain boundaries. Several methods are in existence to estimate the hydrogen content diffused in materials, including vacuum hot extraction method, mercury method, glycerine technique and gas chromatography [ 8 ]. When diffusible hydrogen present in low quantity, Mercury technique is the simplest, cheap and suitable one in comparison to other techniques to quantify the content of diffusible hydrogen. HE depends on the rate of deformation. It has been found that HE is more severe at slow deformation rates. When hydrogen present in the material, several parameters exist which can affect the mechanical behaviour of material, for example (Fig.  1 ).
Fig. 1 Main parameters involved in the HE phenomenon

In metals and alloys, hydrogen-induced damage can appear in various forms, such as hydrogen-induced blistering, hydrogen embrittlement (HE), hydride-induced cracking, hydrogen attack, and cracking resulting from internal hydrogen precipitation [ 8 ,  9 ]. Among these, hydrogen embrittlement is the most common in high-strength materials, particularly steels [ 10 ]. HE occurs when hydrogen atoms enter a material and significantly reduce its strength, often in a hydrogen-rich environment. At the same time, ductility is also diminished, making the material brittle. This embrittlement effect is exacerbated by slow strain rates and elevated temperatures. However, the exact mechanisms behind this degradation remain unclear, and ongoing research continues to explore this phenomenon [ 11 ].

Hydrogen embrittlement adversely affects mechanical characteristics like tensile strength, impact strength, fatigue strength, and ductility. To assess these changes, slow strain rate tests (SSRT) are often performed on hydrogen-charged samples to evaluate their mechanical behaviour under tensile stress [ 12 ]. The interaction between slip bands and hydrogen plays a crucial role in HE [ 13 ], as hydrogen promotes the formation of microcracks along slip bands, thereby accelerating fatigue crack growth [ 14 ].

Hydrogen can enter materials through various processes, including manufacturing, electroplating, cathodic charging, and welding [ 15 ]. In the case of cathodic charging, research shows that the current density is crucial for the absorption of hydrogen into steel. For effective hydrogen charging, the current density should range between 0.02 mA/cm² and 40 mA/cm² [ 16 ], with higher current densities increasing the probability of hydrogen diffusion into the material.

During welding, hydrogen diffusion into the heat-affected zone (HAZ) can lead to hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC). To mitigate this risk, preheating electrodes before welding is recommended to reduce hydrogen absorption in the weld pool. Post-weld heating or treatment is sometimes necessary to minimise HAC. Additionally, research suggests that using negative polarity and low welding current results in lower levels of diffusible hydrogen.

To evaluate hydrogen embrittlement, methods such as Linearly Increasing Stress Test (LIST) and Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS) are commonly used. SSRTs have shown that the presence of hydrogen significantly reduces fracture stress in both notched and smooth specimens [ 17 ]. Microstructural analysis of fractured specimens using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) offers further insights into the damage caused by hydrogen. Preventive measures to reduce hydrogen embrittlement include selecting materials that are less susceptible to HE and applying coatings that minimise hydrogen uptake. These strategies could be beneficial to reduce the risk of embrittlement in critical applications [ 18 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen entry into steel
paragraphs: Hydrogen is a very lightweight element. Hydrogen gas is usually present in its molecular form (H 2 ). The size of the hydrogen molecule is relatively large, making it difficult to diffuse through solid metals. For hydrogen to penetrate into the steel, it must be broken down into individual hydrogen atoms. Hydrogen can penetrate metals either in its gaseous form or through the electrochemical reduction of hydrogen charged specimens in aqueous environments. Hydrogen entry depends on several factors and leads to hydrogen embrittlement. The key parameters influencing hydrogen introduction include the applied current density, electrolyte composition, the potential at the electrolyte-metal interface and pH of the solution. Additional factors, primarily environmental, include temperature, applied pressure and gas purity [ 19 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen gaseous entry
paragraphs: In general, the reactions involve the adsorption of hydrogen in molecular form, which breaks down into hydrogen atoms that are subsequently adsorbed upon the metal surface. These adsorbed hydrogen atoms then diffuse inside the crystal lattice of the metal [ 20 ]. When metals come into contact with a gaseous hydrogen atmosphere, the gas–solid interaction occurs through three main processes: physisorption, chemisorption, and absorption [ 21 ]. These processes are illustrated in Fig.  2 .

At the time of physisorption process, weak Van der Waals forces act between the metal surface and the adsorbate, enabling hydrogen molecules to adsorb directly onto the surface. This process is completely reversible.

In chemisorption, a chemical reaction occurs between a metal surface atom and the adsorbate molecule. The interaction involves short-range forces, generally confined to a single molecular layer. Chemisorption is generally slower than physisorption and might be either slowly reversible or irreversible. This reaction often involves the development of covalent bonds between the surface atom and the adsorbate molecule, resulting in dissociation of hydrogen into atomic form.

In absorption, gas–solid interactions result in the incorporation of chemisorbed species into the crystalline structure of steel, followed by their diffusion. Depending on the entry mechanism, hydrogen can be absorbed either in atomic form or as ions (H⁺) [ 22 ].

Environmental aspects such as hydrogen purity, temperature and hydrogen pressure have a significant impact on hydrogen embrittlement (HE). At high pressures, the susceptibility to HE is largely affected by the diffusivity and solubility of hydrogen within the material.
Fig. 2 Mechanism of hydrogen gas entry in metals

sections.heading: Entry of hydrogen into aqueous phase
paragraphs: The electrochemical process responsible for hydrogen entry into steels in an aqueous solution proceeds through multiple stages. Initially, a charge transfer reaction takes place, resulting in the adsorption of atomic hydrogen.
In the second stage, production of molecular hydrogen occurs through chemical recombination and electrochemical desorption.

A reaction that can occur simultaneously with the desorption process is the introduction of atomic hydrogen into the metal from its adsorbed state on the surface. The kinetics of these reactions are governed by the diffusion rate of hydrogen within the metal. When hydrogen is adsorbed from either the gas phase or an aqueous solution, the incorporated atoms induce distortions in the crystal structure at the metal surface [ 23 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen traps
paragraphs: Atomic hydrogen enters the interstitial lattice sites of metals, where it can take positions of lower potential energy than the regular interstitial sites, leading to its entrapment within the steel. Various microstructural features such as vacancies, solute atoms, vacancy clusters, grain boundaries, dislocation cores, precipitate/matrix interfaces, strain fields around precipitates, internal cracks or voids and inclusion/matrix interfaces serve as hydrogen trapping sites [ 24 ]. These traps reduce hydrogen mobility, delaying its transport through the material. The capacity of a trap to retain hydrogen atoms is governed by its hydrogen binding energy and the activation energy necessary for their release.

Within the crystalline structure, different types of hydrogen, such as interstitial and monoatomic hydrogen dissolved in the steel matrix, show different mobility and solubility, which have different effects on mechanical properties [ 25 ].

Thermal desorption analysis (TDA) is a useful technique for characterising hydrogen traps in different steel microstructures. It examines hydrogen absorption and desorption mechanisms by monitoring the release rate of hydrogen from a specimen under continuous heating. The results provide valuable insights for designing advanced materials with improved resistance to hydrogen embrittlement (HE) [ 26 ,  27 ]. In thermal desorption analysis, hydrogen that is weakly trapped is released at lower temperatures, while hydrogen released at higher temperatures is strongly trapped.

There are numerous known hydrogen traps in steel. Examples include (i) solute atoms, (ii) vacancies, (iii) grain boundaries, (iv) dislocations, (v) precipitates, (vi) external surfaces, (vii) inclusions, (viii) voids and (ix) cracks [ 28 ]. The activation energy associated with these traps is affected by factors such as composition, processing history, defect size and the charging conditions of the steel.
In Tables  1  and  2 , several kinds of physical and chemical traps and their activation energies are displayed [ 29 ,  30 ].

Table 1 Hydrogen physical and chemical traps in metals [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ] Chemical traps Physical traps Dual site occupations of octahedral and tetrahedral sites Vacancy Hydride formation Dislocations Lattice dilatation due to thermal expansion and vacancy formation Interstitial and substitutional impurity atoms Diffusion mechanisms for deviation from Arrhenius relation Grain boundaries Strain and stress field Particles and inclusions in matrix Cleavage and crack

Table 2 Activation energy for different types of hydrogen traps [ 33 ,  34 ,  35 ,  36 – 37 ] Traps types Activation energy (kJ/mol) Grain boundary (reversible) 18.20–19.68 Cementite interlace (reversible) 18.35 Titanium substitutional atom (reversible) 26.05 Micro voids in cold worked Iron 35.15–40.31 Interface of MnS 72.3 Interface of TiC (irreversible) 86.98 Austenite-ferrite interface 52 Carbide interface 67–94 Dislocation (reversible) 26.04 Interface of Fe–Oxide 47.2 Interface of A12O3 78.96

Hydrogen traps are typically categorised into 2 types i.e. reversible and irreversible [ 38 ]. Some studies have examined the influence of these traps on the vulnerability of steel to hydrogen-induced cracking, the specific roles of these traps and the mechanisms responsible for fracture remain incompletely understood.

The effect of each trapping site depends on its activation energy and density. Irreversible trapping sites, characterised by high activation energy, can retain hydrogen for extended periods, leading to hydrogen being referred to as non-diffusible. In contrast, sites with lower activation energy are considered reversible traps, where hydrogen exhibits higher diffusivity [ 39 ].

Trapping sites can form or be altered during thermal and mechanical processes, influenced by factors such as second-phase particle precipitation kinetics, inclusion distribution, dislocation density, grain size variations, dimple formation, and the presence of microcracks [ 39 ]. Reversible traps may significantly affect hydrogen diffusivity and susceptibility to embrittlement, as hydrogen atoms can reside at these sites for shorter durations while exhibiting higher diffusivity [ 40 ]. Materials having a fine dispersion of irreversible traps are less prone to HE [ 41 ].

Additionally, the segregation of carbon, distribution of inclusions, and precipitates (such as NbC, VC, TiC) may enhance hydrogen trapping. Earlier studies suggest that carbide interfaces and incoherent precipitates possess higher trapping energies than grain boundaries and dislocations [ 42 ]. Nonetheless, grain boundaries and dislocations still play a significant role in the mechanisms of hydrogen embrittlement (HE) [ 43 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms
paragraphs: Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) occurs when even little amount of hydrogen causes catastrophic fracture, often triggered by residual stresses or the application of relatively low loads, leading to a loss of ductility or toughness [ 42 ]. Several mechanisms contribute to the HE of materials such as hydrogen-enhanced local plasticity (HELP), hydrogen-enhanced decohesion mechanism (HEDE) and adsorption-induced dislocation emission (AIDE) [ 43 ,  44 ,  45 ,  46 – 47 ]. Table  3  summarises the key mechanisms responsible for hydrogen embrittlement, highlighting their dominant effects on mechanical properties and the characteristic fracture modes associated with each mechanism.

Table 3 Main mechanisms of hydrogen embrittlement, along with their primary effects on material behaviour and the corresponding fracture types observed in steels [ 42 ,  43 ,  44 ,  45 ,  46 – 47 ] Mechanism Main Effect Fracture Type Hydrogen Enhanced Local Plasticity Increases dislocation motion, local plasticity Often trans granular or quasi-cleavage Hydrogen Enhanced Decohesion Weaken atomic bonds, lowers cohesion Intergranular or phase boundary fracture Adsorption-Induced Dislocation Emission Promotes dislocation emission at crack tip Localised plastic deformation near surface
Here are some of the proposed mechanisms:

Hydrogen Enhanced Decohesion Mechanism (HEDE) : This mechanism suggests that hydrogen contributes to brittle fracture by reducing the cohesive strength between the atomic bonds in the metal lattice resulting in brittle failure as shown in Fig.  3  (a). This reduction allows for weakness under tensile loads, facilitating crack propagation and ultimately leading to material failure [ 48 ]. When hydrogen atoms are dispersed throughout the material and external loads are applied, they diffuse into the material and weaken the interatomic bonds, particularly at the crack tip. This weakening decreases the surface energy, leading to a lower fracture stress that results in the failure below the material’s permissible limits. Particularly for high-strength materials, HEDE is most commonly acknowledged when it comes to causing intergranular (Fig.  3  (b)) or phase-boundary failure (Fig.  3  (c)) [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ].
Fig. 3 Schematic diagram of the HEDE mechanism ( a ) in the lattice, ( b ) at a grain boundary, and ( c ) at a phase boundary

Hydrogen Enhanced Local Plasticity (HELP) : In this mechanism, hydrogen accumulation near the crack tip enhances dislocation mobility by lowering the resistance to dislocation movement, resulting in highly localised plastic deformation within the metal lattice [ 49 ]. The mode of fracture may vary and manifest as intergranular, transgranular, or quasi-cleavage, based on the content of hydrogen, the microstructure, and the stress intensity at the crack tip. Fractographic examinations indicate that deformation is restricted to a small portion, leading to reduced macroscopic ductility. The existence of hydrogen reduces the activation energy for dislocation movement and decreases the activation area, thereby facilitating this localised plasticity [ 46 ,  50 ,  51 ,  52 – 53 ]. This mechanism has been observed in various materials, including those with FCC, BCC, and HCP structures, as well as pure and alloyed materials [ 28 ]. Figure  4  illustrates this mechanism.
Fig. 4 Schematic representation of the HELP mechanism

Adsorption Induced Dislocation Emission (AIDE) : This mechanism is similar to the HELP mechanism and also involves localised plasticity. However, the main distinction is the adsorption of solute hydrogen atoms onto the surface, particularly in stress-concentrated regions like crack tips, which induces localised plasticity near the surface [ 54 ]. Hydrogen facilitates the movement of dislocations toward the crack tips, promoting crack growth and intense deformation in the surrounding area. During deformation, hydrogen interacts with dislocations, causing trapped hydrogen to diffuse to regions of greater stress intensity, which induces localised plasticity. In this mechanism, crack initiation and propagation occur due to decohesion and dislocation emission at the crack tip. The combined effects of slip at the micro-void coalescence and at the crack tip lead to crack growth and eventual failure. Figure  5  illustrates this mechanism.
Fig. 5 Schematic of the AIDE mechanism

In a study performed by Wasim et al. [ 55 ], SEM micrographs of the fractured surface of the specimens corroded in both the solution of 5 pH (fracture toughness = 149.9 MPa⋅m 0.5 ) and 2.5 pH (fracture toughness = 138.6 MPa⋅m 0.5 , hydrogen concentration: 2.95 ppm) after 365 days are shown in Fig.  6  (a) and (b), respectively. Both specimens showed similar fracture appearance. However, as seen in Fig.  6  (a), the specimen with higher fracture toughness (149.9 MPa⋅m 0.5 ) mainly showed a mixed quasi-cleavage (QC)-like fracture, where microvoid coalescence (MVC) regions were much more prominent than the transgranular (TG) fracture feature (MVC ≫ TG). In contrast, the specimen with lower fracture toughness (138.6 MPa·m⁰·⁵), shown in Fig.  6  (b), still had MVC as the main fracture mode (MVC > TG), but the TG fracture areas were more widespread. Figure  6  (c) shows a high-magnification SEM image of the fractured surface of the lower fracture toughness specimen (138.6 MPa·m⁰·⁵) after corrosion in a 2.5 pH solution for 365 days. In the mainly TG regions, a local decohesion at particular grain boundaries and triple junctions, micro-fissures, and initial intergranular (IG) microcracks can be observed.

Fig. 6 SEM micrograph of the fractured surface of specimens: ( a ) corroded in pH = 5 solution for 365 days, fracture toughness = 149.9 MPa⋅m 0.5  ( b ) corroded in pH = 2.5 solution for 365 days, fracture toughness = 138.6 MPa⋅m 0.5  ( c ) higher magnification image of specimen corroded in 2.5 pH solution with fracture toughness = 138.6 MPa⋅m 0.5  [ 55 ]

sections.heading: Hydrogen embrittlement in materials
paragraphs: Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) is a widely recognised phenomenon that impacts high-strength materials, particularly steels. It refers to the deterioration of mechanical properties caused by the entry of hydrogen. The detrimental effects of hydrogen on steel have been acknowledged for over a century. HE can reduce a material’s ultimate tensile strength, fracture strength, fracture toughness, ductility and fatigue strength [ 56 ]. The term “embrittlement” describes the transition from ductile to brittle behaviour, which can lead to failure at stress levels below the yield or tensile stress. In some cases, HE can cause a decrease in ductility without affecting yield or tensile strength. Over time, different terms have been used to denote HE, depending on the context [ 28 ,  57 ]. For instance, Internal Hydrogen Embrittlement (IHE) refers to embrittlement caused by hydrogen that is pre-existing or inherent in the steel, while Hydrogen Environment Embrittlement (HEE) is caused by external hydrogen introduced during service. The term Hydrogen-Assisted Cracking (HAC) is also commonly employed, sometimes with qualifiers like “internal” or “external.” Specific industries use their own terminology for HE. In the field of welding, Hydrogen-Assisted Cold Cracking (HACC) refers to weld failures after cooling to atmospheric temperatures. Environmental Hydrogen Embrittlement (EHE) refers to fractures that occur in cathodically protected structures, while Hydrogen-Assisted Fatigue (HAF) describes hydrogen-induced fractures during cyclic loading in the corrosion industry.

HE susceptibility varies among materials. High-strength steels, high Mn-steels, aluminium alloys, titanium, magnesium, and their alloys are particularly vulnerable [ 54 ,  58 ,  59 – 60 ]. Steels, widely used in structural applications that require both strength and ductility, become increasingly susceptible to HE as their tensile strength increases. This limits the use of high and ultra-high-strength steels in certain applications, despite their advantages in aerospace, automotive, nuclear, and hydrogen storage industries [ 61 ,  62 – 63 ].

Bainitic steel, which offers excellent strength, ductility, toughness, and fatigue resistance, is particularly prone to hydrogen embrittlement due to its chemical composition. Recent research has shown that partially replacing silicon with aluminium improves bainitic steel’s overall performance, significantly reducing HE susceptibility and enhancing its resistance to delayed fracture. A comparison between bainitic steel with a granular microstructure and tempered martensitic steel revealed that granular bainite has a larger extrinsic resistance to HE. Specifically, when both steels were hydrogen-charged at the same current density, granular bainite absorbed less hydrogen than tempered martensitic steel. However, in terms of intrinsic HE resistance (which compares samples with similar diffusible hydrogen content), tempered-martensite steel outperforms granular bainite, as hydrogen tends to concentrate in martensite islands and retained austenite within the bainite structure. Additionally, granular bainitic steels with lower sulphur content demonstrate better resistance to HE because sulphur destroys grain boundary strength. Because extrinsic properties are more relevant to industrial applications, granular bainitic steels are considered appropriate for use in hydrogen environments due to their superior extrinsic HE resistance [ 64 ].

sections.heading: Classification of hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Hydrogen embrittlement (HE) can be categorised into two main types:

Subcritical crack growth below the yield stress threshold : This occurs when cracks propagate at stress levels lower than the yield stress. Fracture initiation between the yield stress and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) : In this case, fractures can initiate either through microvoid coalescence or brittle failure mechanism, often starting at the surface of the material.

The existence of defects within the material plays a critical role in initiating cracks. If operating conditions such as applied loads or exposure to a hydrogen environment vary, these cracks can grow until they reach a critical length, at which point their propagation becomes unstable, leading to material failure.
Subcritical Crack Growth .

In situations where hydrogen content is large at the crack tip, absorption of hydrogen accelerates HE, and the crack begins to propagate. Hydrogen weakens the material’s fracture resistance, promoting subcritical crack growth [ 65 ]. The crack growth is often because of chemical corrosion at the crack tip and resembles stress corrosion cracking (SCC) [ 66 ,  67 ]. When the rate of passive film formation at the crack tip surpasses the rate of dissolution, the progression of crack growth slows down. Subcritical crack growth persists until the crack reaches a critical length, at which the stress intensity factor becomes critical, triggering unstable crack propagation. Subcritical crack growth takes place when the applied stress intensity factor (KI) surpasses the threshold value (KIH) [ 68 ]. However, with crack propagation, however, the stress intensity factor gradually decreases [ 69 ].

There is a threshold stress beyond which subcritical crack growth can occur. This threshold varies between materials but is generally lower than the material’s yield stress [ 70 ,  71 – 72 ]. In some cases, this threshold is around one-third of the material’s fracture stress, but it decreases with a slower rate of applied stress [ 73 ].

The loading rate plays a significant role in diffusion of hydrogen; at high loads, effect of hydrogen is minimal, while at low loads, hydrogen has more time to diffuse into the metal, facilitating subcritical crack growth. Thus, low loading rates are associated with subcritical crack growth [ 66 ,  74 ].
Fracture Initiation between Yield Stress and UTS .

Once a crack grows to an appropriate length, reaching the critical crack length as defined by Griffith, fracture occurs at stress levels below the material’s ultimate tensile strength (UTS). If the hydrogen concentration is high, brittle fracture occurs, which severely affects the material’s mechanical properties. On the other hand, if hydrogen has a lesser impact, ductile failure may result [ 66 ,  75 ]. Fracture initiation can occur either through microvoid coalescence or a brittle fracture mode, such as intergranular or transgranular fracture [ 68 ,  69 ].

When a crack grows to a critical length, its propagation becomes unstable, and the stress intensity factor reaches a critical value, termed the critical stress intensity factor (Kc). The most widely used form of Kc is the fracture toughness (KIC), which represents a specific value of the stress intensity factor [ 76 ].

For a delayed fracture to occur, a combination of stress and hydrogen concentration is necessary. At high stress levels, multiple microcracks form and eventually coalesce into voids, ultimately leading to final failure [ 77 ]. Examination of the fracture surface through fractography reveals mixed-mode failure, with some areas displaying microvoid dimples characteristic of ductile fracture, while others exhibit brittle features, such as “fish-eye” formations surrounded by microvoid coalescence (MVC).

sections.heading: Characteristics of hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: The key characteristic of HE is its sensitivity to strain rate and the material’s susceptibility to delayed failure. At higher strain rates, materials are less prone to HE, while slower strain rates tend to enhance the effects of HE, increasing the likelihood of delayed failure. The susceptibility to HE is primarily due to hydrogen diffusion and dislocation movement within steel and alloys, facilitating the transport of hydrogen atoms [ 17 ].

HE is a well-known issue in high-strength materials, where catastrophic failure can occur at stress levels below the material’s expected strength. Understanding fracture mechanics is crucial to predicting how cracks might propagate in a material under the influence of hydrogen or corrosion reactions, as corrosion can generate hydrogen atoms. The presence of hydrogen makes the material brittle, and crack growth occurs either through dislocation emission or microvoid coalescence (MVC). In some cases, both mechanisms can act together, leading to crack growth and eventual fracture of the material below its permissible stress limit.

Studying fracture mechanics helps understand crack growth behaviour and rate in materials exposed to hydrogen. Additionally, various crack growth mechanisms need to be investigated to understand hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC), which refers to subcritical crack growth driven by HE.

sections.heading: Role of microstructure in hydrogen embrittlement
paragraphs: Microstructure significantly influences hydrogen embrittlement (HE) susceptibility. While ferritic steels are generally resistant to HE, they lack the necessary strength, leading to the intentional formation of pearlite during manufacturing. Pearlite, which consists of both ferrite and cementite, offers increased strength but is also harder and more brittle, making it more vulnerable to HE. Additionally, non-metallic inclusions and harder microstructures like bainite and martensite can serve as potential sites for crack propagation. As opposed to, acicular ferrite helps to inhibit crack initiation and propagation due to its softer nature [ 78 ,  79 – 80 ]. During heat treatment, various microstructural combinations, including bainitic ferrite, ferrite-pearlite, and polygonal ferrite-bainitic ferrite are formed [ 81 ,  82 ]. Certain phases, like bainite, coarse pearlite, martensite and fine pearlite, demonstrate high hydrogen trapping efficiency, increasing their susceptibility to HE [ 83 ,  84 ].

In a comparative study of three types of steel having microstructure, ferrite + bainite, ferrite + martensite/austenite, and ferrite + martensite, different crack propagation patterns were observed after hydrogen charging. In the ferrite + bainite sample, cracks propagated along the band-like structures formed by the bainite [ 85 ], which can trap hydrogen atoms and potentially lead to brittle failure [ 83 ]. Hydrogen diffusion occurs at the interfaces between the bainite and ferritic matrix, initiating cracks when critical hydrogen concentrations are reached. In the ferrite + martensite/austenite microstructure, cracks propagated along the ferrite matrix and the martensite/austenite islands. Similarly, in the ferrite + martensite sample, cracks were observed along both the martensite and ferrite phases, as well as within the martensite itself. Specimens with ferrite + bainite and ferrite + martensite/austenite microstructures exhibited greater resistance to HE than the specimen with a ferrite + martensite microstructure out of the three investigated specimens.

In dual-phase steels containing martensite and bainite of different morphologies obtained by the conventional or thermomechanical heat-treatment, the susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement was investigated by electrolytic hydrogen charging. The results showed that finer microstructure has lower susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement. The fractographic analysis showed that quasicleavage and dimple fracture mode was obtained in the hydrogen-charged samples for both treating processes. The quasicleavage facet of the thermomechanical treated samples is smaller than that of the conventional heated ones (Fig.  7 ). It has been found that hydrogen can be trapped at lath boundaries, leading to crack initiation once a critical hydrogen level is achieved [ 86 ].
Fig. 7 Hydrogen-charged SEM fractographs of dual-phase steel for two heat-treatments: ( a ) conventional heat-treatment; ( b ) thermomechanical heat-treatment. B/M: bainite or martensite [ 86 ]

In a study, the mechanical properties of thermomechanically treated steel samples were investigated in the presence of hydrogen [ 87 ]. The ultimate tensile strength and yield strength of the samples with and without hydrogen (charging till saturation) are comparable (Fig.  8 (a), (b), and (c)). The hydrogen-charged sample austempered at 430 ℃ with 8% strain had the highest ultimate tensile strength and yield strength compared to other conditions (Fig.  8 (e)). However, the ductility of the strained samples with charged hydrogen (till saturation) had been decreased to three times for all transformation temperatures. The ductility of the unstrained sample transformed at 475 ℃ had been decreased to nine times (Fig.  8 (f)). The thermomechanically treated samples are charged with 1.5 ppm of hydrogen and then subjected to mechanical testing. The ductility of the hydrogen-charged sample austempered at 475 ℃ with 8% strain was superior to other austempered temperatures in all the cases (Fig.  8 (d)).

The fractography of the hydrogen-free samples revealed ductile fracture with several dimples (Fig.  9 (a), (b), and (c)). The hydrogen-charged samples showed the brittle failure with quasi cleavage and facets in the fracture surface as shown in Fig.  9 (d), (e) and (f) [ 87 ].

Fig. 8 Tensile behaviour of hydrogen-free samples and hydrogen charged samples corresponding to the bainitic transformation with 8% strain during quenching, held at ( a ) 475 ℃, ( b ) 450 ℃ and ( c ) 430 ℃, ( d ) tensile behaviour of samples charged with 1.5 PPM of hydrogen ( e ) ultimate tensile strength and yield strength for samples with and without hydrogen charging, ( f ) tensile elongation of the samples with and without hydrogen charging [ 87 ]

Fig. 9 Fracture surface of hydrogen-free samples ( a ,  b ,  c ) and hydrogen charged samples ( d ,  e ,  f ) corresponding to the bainitic transformation with 8% strain during quenching, held at 475 ℃, 450 ℃ and 430 ℃ respectively [ 87 ]

Norouzi et al. [ 88 ] studied the effect of plastic deformations on the hydrogen embrittlement (HE) of transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) steel. In situ tensile tests showed that with increasing hydrogen current density, the total ductility loss increased to approximately 37% compared to an uncharged specimen (Fig.  10 ).
Fig. 10 Tensile engineering stress-strain curves before and after hydrogen charging [ 88 ]

In a study, Rajput et al. [ 89 ] investigated the effect of hydrogen on the ductility of TWIP, TRIP and DP steels and compared it with uncharged material (Fig.  11 (a-d)). Figure  11  showed that as the time of hydrogen charging was increased, tensile strain was reduced significantly for all kind of steels. Such a loss in ductility was primarily attributed to the gradual disappearance of the necking phenomenon with increasing hydrogen charging, which is reflected in a brittle transition of fracture behaviour.

Fracture surfaces of the uncharged and 168 h hydrogen charged specimens has been shown in Fig.  12 (a-d) [ 89 ]. Fracture surfaces of all the steels in uncharged condition revealed overall characteristic of ductile fracture. However, the fracture surface of the hydrogen charged X60Mn22 and X30MnAl22-1 steels showed quasi-cleavage and intergranular brittle fracture in the hydrogen diffused zone close to its faying surface (Fig.  12 (a), (b)). But the depth of quasi-cleavage fracture zone in X30MnAl22-1 steel is relatively less as compared to that observed in case of the X60Mn22 steel. The Quasi-cleavage fracture was also observed in the hydrogen charged zone of the TRIP 800 steel (Fig.  12 (c)). Some brittle facets are observed in the sub-surface and also in the region further below the sub-surface. This is assumed to be attributed to transformation of retained austenite into martensite. The fracture surface of the hydrogen pre-charged DP 780 steel showed quasi-cleavage fracture with some micro-cracks in the surface zone (Fig.  12 (d)). Substantial brittle facets were also observed in the sub-surface.

Fig. 12 SEM images of uncharged and hydrogen pre-charged ( a ) X60Mn22, ( b ) X30MnAl22-1, ( c ) TRIP 800 and ( d ) DP 780 steels fractured in slow strain rate test [ 89 ]

sections.heading: Hydrogen charging characteristic and tools to measure HE
paragraphs: To determine the content of hydrogen present in a material during experimental investigations, hydrogen charging is essential. This charging can typically be performed through electrochemical methods (cathodic charging) or by using high-pressure hydrogen gas. These methods facilitate hydrogen diffusion within the material, which can lead to degradation of its properties and cause hydrogen embrittlement [ 15 ]. Within the material, there are specific sites that act as hydrogen traps, where hydrogen atoms can accumulate. These traps are classified as reversible and irreversible. Thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) is employed to estimate the amount of hydrogen within the material, whether in the charging process or in gaseous conditions.

sections.heading: Hydrogen charging method
paragraphs: To assess HE susceptibility, hydrogen must be introduced into the material through charging. Three primary hydrogen charging methods are used: cathodic charging [ 89 ], immersion in an aqueous solution at free corrosion potential, and exposure to a corrosive atmospheric environment. The Schematic representation of cathodic and immersion-type charging is shown in Fig.  13 . Among these methods, immersion is often preferred because it allows for the uniform charging of multiple specimens simultaneously, even for larger and more complex shapes. However, a drawback of the immersion method is that the specimens may dissolve in the solution, altering their surface conditions during testing.

In this study, an immersion-type hydrogen charging procedure was used that minimizes specimen dissolution. The charging solution used was ammonium thiocyanate (NH₄SCN), that is well recognized for evaluating hydrogen embrittlement in steels. The impact of NH₄SCN concentration on the amount of diffusible hydrogen and HE resistance was investigated. The results showed that amount of diffusible hydrogen increased with higher concentrations of the NH₄SCN solution.
Fig. 13 Schematic representation of hydrogen charging process ( a ) cathodic charging ( b ) immersion-type charging

sections.heading: Linearly increasing stress test (LIST)
paragraphs: Mechanical testing methods are essential for evaluating hydrogen embrittlement in materials. Initially, constant load tests and constant extension tests were commonly employed to assess the effects of HE. Both methods focus on determining the threshold limit of stress, which can be defined as the value of stress below which no failure happens [ 90 ]. However, a challenge with these tests is that components may not fail within a specific timeframe, often requiring a lengthy period before fracture.

To address this, a new technique known as the constant extension rate test (CERT), also referred to as slow strain rate testing (SSRT), was introduced [ 91 ]. In this method, a constant rate of elongation is applied over time until the sample fractures. A limitation of CERT is that once the threshold stress is reached, the specimen may extend for a prolonged period before failure.

To overcome this issue, linearly increasing stress testing (LIST) was developed. This method is same as CERT but offers distinct advantages. In LIST, the sample is stressed in gradually increasing manner until fracture occurs. A load is applied by the motion of a weight, with the rate of motion governed by a motor. Figure  14  illustrates the schematic of the LIST method. While CERT is primarily a displacement-controlled method, LIST is load-controlled [ 70 ]. Literature indicates that both CERT and LIST yield similar threshold stress values; however, with LIST, the specimen typically fails soon after reaching the threshold stress, allowing for a more efficient test completion [ 43 ].
Fig. 14 Schematic representation of the linear increasing stress test (LIST) apparatus

sections.heading: Thermal desorption spectroscopy
paragraphs: Thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) is a well-established technique for investigating HE and hydrogen-related failure in materials [ 92 ,  93 – 94 ]. Several techniques exist for measuring diffusible hydrogen in steel, and understanding hydrogen mobility is crucial in HE studies [ 95 ]. TDS is primarily employed to qualify and quantify the content of diffusible hydrogen.

In TDS, the amount of desorbed hydrogen is determined through controlled and limited heating. Steel contains trapping sites that facilitate hydrogen accumulation. As the steel is heated, the absorbed thermal energy allows hydrogen to escape when it reaches a specific threshold known as the desorption activation energy. The temperature at which hydrogen atoms are released is referred to as the desorption temperature. The quantity of desorbed hydrogen is then measured using quadrupole mass spectrometry [ 96 ]. One of TDS’s notable advantages is its high sensitivity, enabling it to accurately detect very low levels of desorbed hydrogen, as low as 0.1 mg/kg [ 50 ,  97 ,  98 ]. When combined with other testing methods, TDS can enhance hydrogen embrittlement detection and offer a deeper insight into the mechanisms driving HE.

Figure  15  illustrates the TDS process. TDS test was carried out within 10 min after the completion of hydrogen charging. The specimen was heated from atmospheric temperature to 800 °C at a constant heating rate of 100 °C/h, unless otherwise indicated. A quadrupolar mass spectrometer was used to analyse the diffusing hydrogen out of the sample and hydrogen content can be obtained by the integration of the hydrogen evolution curve [ 99 ].
Fig. 15 Schematic representation of the TDS analysis

TDS analysis was performed on both uncharged and hydrogen charged cold deformed, annealed specimens of cold hardened bainitic steel. The findings showed that in addition to the initial high-temperature peak seen in the as-rolled specimen, the hydrogen-charged cold-drawn sample also shows an additional low-temperature desorption peak. This resulted to a substantial increase in the absorbed hydrogen content. For the uncharged specimen, the hydrogen desorption curve exhibits a single peak at approximately 320 °C, whereas the hydrogen-charged specimen shows two distinct desorption peaks at around 150 °C and 320 °C [ 99 ].

sections.heading: Hydrogen permeation test
paragraphs: Permeation testing is one of the simplest techniques for measuring diffusible hydrogen in steel. By quantifying diffusible hydrogen, the susceptibility of steel to HE can be assessed. For effective implementation of the permeation test, it is often combined with other testing methods [ 100 ].

The permeation test uses a double-cell arrangement composed of a charging (entry) cell and an oxidation (exit) cell, separated by a steel membrane [ 101 ,  102 ]. In this setup, hydrogen is introduced into the charging cell through an electrochemical reaction in a suitable electrolyte, after which it diffuses through the membrane into the oxidation cell. The hydrogen concentration on the entry side is regulated using either potentiostatic or galvanostatic control. The exit cell, typically filled with an electrolyte such as 0.1 M NaOH, is maintained at an anodic potential to promote oxidation of the diffusing hydrogen. This oxidation process releases electrons, which are measured as an output current. To minimize interference from competing oxidation reactions and to enhance the catalytic activity for hydrogen oxidation, the exit surface of the steel membrane is commonly coated with nickel or palladium [ 103 ,  104 ]. Figure  16  illustrates the schematic representation of the permeation setup.
Fig. 16 Schematic representation of a typical double-cell permeation set-up

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: Microstructural analysis is essential for evaluating the susceptibility of materials and alloys to hydrogen embrittlement (HE). To investigate the internal microstructure and the effects of hydrogen, SEM and TEM are generally used analytical techniques. SEM is user-friendly, versatile, and often preferred for its straightforward sample preparation compared to other methods [ 105 ]. Additionally, SEM provides three-dimensional images and is effective in examining fracture features such as micro voids, shear dimples, and hydrogen fisheyes [ 106 ]. It can also be combined with other characterization techniques, like energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), enhancing its analytical capabilities. A minor drawback of scanning electron microscopy is its relatively low magnification and resolution in comparison to more advanced microscopy techniques. Nevertheless, it is widely used for fractographic studies and surface imaging applications.

In contrast, TEM is a more powerful technique, offering higher magnification and resolution than SEM. It provides valuable information on morphology, topography, and crystallography. However, for TEM experiment, samples should be electron transparent having thickness less than 90 nm for effective microstructural analysis.

sections.heading: Hydrogen microprint technique (HMT)
paragraphs: This technique is employed to trace the paths of diffusible hydrogen in metals. By identifying these paths, specific microstructural features accompanying with hydrogen’s effects can be determined. The hydrogen mapping technique (HMT) is known for its simplicity and unique ability to provide high accuracy and resolution [ 107 ,  108 ]. HMT has been utilized to examine hydrogen distribution in stress fields, especially in notched and deformed steel. This technique is applicable to different kind of materials, including high-strength steel, low-carbon steel, and austenitic stainless steel [ 109 ,  110 ]. In this technique, a thin layer of AgBr gel is coated onto the surface of the hydrogen-charged specimen. As hydrogen diffuses out of the metal, it reacts with the silver salt, forming metallic silver that indicates the sites of hydrogen emission. Silver particles accumulate at these points, while any unreacted gel is later removed. The specimen is then analysed using SEM to identify hydrogen exit sites indicated by the deposited silver [ 111 ].The schematic representation of microprinting technique is shown in Fig.  17 .
Fig. 17 Schematic of the microprinting technique

sections.heading: HE prevention
paragraphs: To effectively prevent hydrogen embrittlement (HE) in high-strength materials, understanding the sources of hydrogen and the mechanisms responsible for HE is crucial. The selection of appropriate materials is important when operating in hydrogen-rich environments. Materials should have lower strength and higher resistance to HE. Additionally, proper material design is essential and features such as notches, sharp edges, and irregular surfaces should be avoided, and residual stresses must be eliminated before further processing [ 112 ]. Heat treatment is often used to remove absorbed hydrogen, which can otherwise lead to material damage or failure. The specifics of the heat treatment process, including the heating temperature, depend on the material being treated. For example, tempering at 500 °C has been shown to improve HE resistance and reduce susceptibility in hot-rolled bainitic rail steel without significantly compromising strength and ductility. To further reduce the risk of HE, pickling processes are used to remove scale and oxide products using acidic solutions [ 113 ]. However, since acids promote hydrogen diffusion, mechanical methods like sandblasting, grit blasting, and vapor blasting are preferred to minimize this risk.

HE prevention can also be achieved by alloying base materials with other metals and applying protective coatings. Materials like platinum (Pt), copper (Cu), nickel (Ni), niobium, silver, aluminium and graphene are commonly employed as protective coatings to form a thin layer on the surface, which helps in reducing hydrogen permeation into steel and other alloys [ 114 ,  115 ]. Gold (Au), tin (Sn), and certain tin-lead (Sn-Pb) alloys are also highly operative as barriers to hydrogen penetration [ 116 ,  117 ]. Techniques like electrodeposition, vacuum deposition, organic coatings, and mechanical plating aid in this regard. Using effective inhibitors is another important strategy. Cadmium, for instance, serves as a protective barrier to hinder hydrogen diffusion in steel, particularly in marine environments, though its toxicity limits its use. Cadmium and tin have lower hydrogen diffusion coefficients compared to ferrite (Fig.  18 ). Cadmium or zinc electroplating is often used on high-strength steels for corrosion protection, though this process introduces hydrogen into the steel. To allow hydrogen to escape, a “de-embrittling” heat treatment is performed at 180–240 °C for 7–24 h, provided this does not negatively affect the material’s mechanical properties [ 118 ,  119 ]. However, mixing zinc with nickel decreases penetration of hydrogen [ 119 ] because nickel forms a diffusion barrier [ 120 ]. Nickel coating is effective for this purpose as the hydrogen diffusivity in nickel at room temperature is much lower than in ferrite (Fig.  18 ).

Other metal coatings such as platinum, copper, cadmium, silver, aluminium and gold can also inhibit hydrogen diffusion into steel. Additionally, oxide and nitride surface layers serve as barriers against hydrogen entry. Alumina (aluminium oxide) is another material that acts as an obstacle against hydrogen diffusion. Plasma deposition techniques are used to apply alumina coatings to steel, and these coatings have been found to significantly reduce hydrogen penetration [ 121 ]. In some cases, hydrogen traps within the material can limit hydrogen diffusion by concentrating hydrogen in specific areas. While the hydrogen concentration is higher in these trapped regions, it does not cause harm to the material [ 121 ].

Some studies suggest that corrosion products on the material surface can also act as barriers to hydrogen ingress [ 112 ]. Service conditions play a key role in HE susceptibility as well. Localised stress in coatings can lead to their degradation, allowing hydrogen to diffuse into the underlying metal [ 122 ].

A critical concentration of diffusible hydrogen, denoted as Hc, exists below which fracture does not occur. This value can be determined from experiments. If the hydrogen content remains below Hc, delayed fractures or failures during service conditions can be avoided [ 121 ,  123 ]. Thus, HE primarily leads to delayed fracture in steel and alloys.

sections.heading: Novel contribution and framework of the present review
paragraphs: This review gives a systematic classification of hydrogen embrittlement behaviour in different types of automotive steels such as martensitic, bainitic, TRIP, and dual-phase (DP) steels, considering both microstructure and fracture behaviour. It also presents an integrated summary framework in Table  5  that connects the main hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms with common testing techniques (SSRT, LIST, TDS) and practical mitigation approaches like alloying, coatings, and microstructure control. This review also provides comparative insights into how various microstructural features such as grain boundaries, dislocations, and precipitates affect hydrogen trapping and diffusion, which are often discussed separately in earlier works. Finally, the paper offers a practical perspective by summarising prevention methods most relevant to the automotive industry, including proper heat treatment, protective coatings, and careful material selection.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This paper addresses materials susceptible to hydrogen penetration and diffusion, the causes and mechanisms leading to deterioration in mechanical properties, and hydrogen-based failures like hydrogen embrittlement (HE) and hydrogen-induced cracking. Additionally, it explores prevention methods that can reduce or eliminate hydrogen penetration, creating barriers that help minimize the risk of HE. The key conclusions of this study are given below:

Diffusible hydrogen is a primary factor which can be responsible for hydrogen embrittlement in materials in the form of delayed fractures. When the diffusible hydrogen content remains below the critical hydrogen concentration (Hc), the risk of HE is low. HE is likely to occur when the hydrogen concentration exceeds the threshold value. Proper material selection is crucial for reducing HE susceptibility, and heat treatment processes can be applied to restore materials to their actual condition. HE prevention can also be achieved by alloying base materials with elements like copper and aluminium, which reduce hydrogen diffusion. Diffusion layers, such as oxides, nitrides, and carbides, can act as barriers to hydrogen penetration in steels, thereby lowering HE susceptibility. Platinum, nickel, niobium and graphene coatings are efficient in forming protective layers over materials, serving as barriers to hydrogen diffusion. Consequently, these are highly efficient in preventing HE. Hydrogen traps and corrosion products can also act as barriers, preventing hydrogen entry on the material surface.

However, the exact mechanisms responsible for HE remains unclear and are still debated. In many cases, a combination of mechanisms contributes to hydrogen-induced failure. Additionally, there is a disconnect between experiments at the laboratory level and real-world conditions, as laboratory tests are conducted under controlled environments, while materials in hydrogen environments may face more complex situations. Further investigation is required to better understand these mechanisms and to bridge the gap between experimental results and actual working conditions.
